primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The Z alpha-1 antitrypsin variant misfolds and polymerizes within hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, causing toxic intracellular accumulation and liver disease. Reduced secretion simultaneously lowers circulating AAT, permitting neutrophil-elastase-mediated alveolar destruction in the lung.
vignette: A young nonsmoker has basilar panacinar emphysema and chronic liver disease. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes. Genotyping shows homozygous PI*Z SERPINA1 alleles.
lead: Which mechanism most directly causes the hepatic injury in this disorder?
correct: Polymerization and retention of misfolded Z alpha-1 antitrypsin within the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum
distractors: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of hepatocyte alpha-1 antitrypsin receptors
Excess neutrophil elastase directly digesting hepatocyte extracellular matrix
Failure of lysosomal copper export causing oxidative hepatocyte injury
Defective mitochondrial beta-oxidation causing microvesicular steatosis
distractor_notes: AAT deficiency is not caused by autoantibodies against a hepatocyte receptor; the Z allele causes abnormal protein folding and intracellular polymer accumulation.
Unopposed neutrophil elastase is central to lung injury, not the direct hepatocellular mechanism of liver disease.
Defective copper export from hepatocytes is the ATP7B/Wilson disease mechanism.
Mitochondrial beta-oxidation defects can cause microvesicular steatosis but do not produce PAS-positive diastase-resistant AAT globules.
key_expl: The Z variant of alpha-1 antitrypsin has a dual disease mechanism. In the liver, abnormal AAT molecules polymerize and are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, producing a toxic gain-of-function injury. In the lung, reduced secretion creates a loss of antiprotease protection, allowing neutrophil elastase to damage alveolar walls.
objective: Distinguish the hepatic gain-of-function mechanism of PI*ZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency—ER polymer accumulation—from the pulmonary loss-of-function mechanism.
